caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No. It was gypsum, carved to order.

In 1868 New York tobacconist George Hull hired men to quarry a block of gypsum at Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling them it was for a Lincoln monument. The block went to a Chicago stonecutter, and two sculptors carved a ten-foot man modelled on Hull himself. A geologist told him hair would not petrify, so the figure has none. Its skin was beaten with steel knitting needles set in a board to fake pores, then rubbed with sulphuric acid for age.

It was buried on his cousin William Newell's farm in late November 1868. Nearly a year later, on 16 October 1869, hired well-diggers found it. Newell charged fifty cents for fifteen minutes; three to five hundred people came a day.

Cornell's first president, Andrew D. White, noticed there was no reason to dig a well there — good water already ran near the house and barn. Yale's O. C. Marsh called it "a most decided humbug": soluble gypsum with fresh tool marks. Hull confessed on 10 December 1869, saying he had always meant the hoax to be exposed. On 2 February 1870 a court declared both the giant and Barnum's plaster copy fakes.

Still unresolved: whether the Chicago stonecutter knew what he was making. And the copy in a Michigan arcade is Barnum's only because its owner says so.

Images: an 1869 lithograph of "The Onondaga Giant" (Popular Graphic Arts); a Bain News Service negative of the giant, 1910; and both faces of an 1873 stereocard of Cardiff Glen, Fort Dodge, Iowa, scanned by the New York Public Library. All public domain.
